p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for almost two years, and the crew launches January 9.
At the readiness board in December he refused to sign Tallgrass's waiver calling the valve's ground runs nominal, and filed his reasons in writing.
Ruth Calder told the board in public how she signed the Petrel's waiver in 2035, and Garrett put his own 2059 phone call to Hana into the record.

The board deferred the choice to a final test of MOIV-1 on orbit on January 30, with criteria published first, a replacement valve flying up with the crew, and crew risk accepted only by the board with the crew's written consent.
Sam told Ada everything about Leo Marchetti and the jet in Arizona, including that he'll never know.
Quinn Abernathy. Sam's deputy and the countdown lead.
Yusra Haddad. Halcyon's commander, and now the product owner of the flight software backlog.
Ruth Calder. On the readiness board.
Esther Quayle. Chair of the Independent Readiness Board, with thirty years on a range safety console.
Lorna Whitcombe. The ARA's flight operations director.
Dr. Anjali Rao. The doctor on Halcyon's crew.
Ada Okafor. Sam's daughter on Ares Station.
Hollis Bayne. Director of Ares Station.
Chiamaka Okonkwo. Breather operations lead on Ares Station.
Thandi Mokoena. Leads the agency's independent verification and validation team for Halcyon's software.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Arlo Dunn. Stand technician, now at Wendell's console.
Corinne Mathers. Leads the new merged Integration and Test team of sixty seven.
Simon Greaves. Runs the Countdown to Ares feed.
Frances Odum. Chair of Families of Ares.
Tuesday, January 2. 5:40 AM. The high bay at Watkins was empty, which Sam had known it would be, and he walked into it anyway.

All three modules had gone by the first week of December, and the floor where they'd stood for three years was swept and bare, with the yellow tape of their footprints still on the epoxy. The overhead crane was parked at the north wall with its hook drawn all the way up. Somebody had left the pallet jack Garrett gave his speeches from in the middle of the floor, and it looked like a thing that had been forgotten at a party.
Over the doors the clock said 47.

Mars was a little over thirteen minutes away by light this morning, and getting closer every day, the way it had been since summer. The crew had been in quarantine at the Cape since the day after Christmas, all four of them in crew quarters with a window onto a parking lot, and Haddad had sent a photograph on New Year's Eve of her four kids on the other side of the glass, holding up a sign that said 2063 in glitter.
He'd spent New Year's Eve at the kitchen table in Aurora, with page thirteen and a pencil. The envelope to Ruth was still on the counter by the door, under his keys, unsealed.

Across the road in the program room, Quinn had the whiteboard the way she'd left it before Christmas. TEST TUE JAN 30, boxed. Under it, since Sunday, a second line in her small capitals. CRITERIA BEFORE DATA. WED 0900, FEDERAL BUILDING. Under that, in Hana's handwriting: Write the limit before you see the trace.
Ruth's Console Log, page fourteen: Nerve.

Ruth's console log. Petrel. After. L Plus 366 Days. June 12 2036. oh four ten, cape. beach road. rental car. parked where the vans parked last year. nobody here. oh four thirty, walked to the water. lifeguard stand. number 7. sat on the step. oh four thirty five, 366. leap year. a year and a day. it took the year a day longer to get here. oh six hundred, the poll. said the stations in order, out loud, to the water. prop first. left a second where the second was. oh six thirty one, liftoff, a year ago. a pelican went over. I let it. oh nine twenty one, ignition. 0938 cutoff. sat through it. oh nine thirty nine, LOS. said it. nobody on the loop. ten hundred, wrote the report in one line. 400 pages. one line. ten oh one, we had the data. we didn't have the nerve. eleven hundred, a woman with a dog asked if I was all right. eleven hundred, said yes. heard how I said it. eleven oh one, said no. eleven oh two, she sat down. the dog too. we didn't talk. thirteen hundred, drove back. 1001 line stands.

I went back on the anniversary because I didn't know what else to do with the day. I'd been told by kind people that it would help. It didn't, particularly. But I wrote the 1001 line on that step, and it's the truest thing in the binder, so the drive was worth it.

We had the data. That's the part people get wrong about the Petrel, when they get it at all. They think we didn't know. We knew the valve had chattered on cycle three. We knew the retests ran warm, or one of us did. We knew its maker had asked for three weeks. All of it was written down, in our own building, months before June. What we didn't have was the nerve to do what the data said when the data said it, because by then the date was in the room and the date had more friends than the data did.

This chapter is about storing nerve in advance. That's what go/no-go criteria are, if you write them properly: a decision made on a calm day, by people who can still think, about what they'll do on a hard day when they can't. It's also about the readiness reviews that keep a ship honest in its last month, about compressing a schedule without squeezing the one thing that tells you the truth, about measuring whether the whole effort did any good, and about what to do when you find out somebody's been hiding something good.

How the exam asks it. When a high stakes test or gate is coming, the PMI answer sets measurable criteria, and what each outcome triggers, before the data exist. "Let's see the results and decide" is the distractor.

The Standard describes phase gates in its section on life cycles, 4.1. A gate is a review that checks whether a phase's exit criteria have been met before the next phase starts, and the exit criteria can be tied to acceptance criteria, contract terms, performance targets, or other tangible measures. Then it lists what can come out of the comparison: go on, go on with changes, end the phase, stay in it, repeat part of it, or park the project. A go/no-go decision has more than two answers, and it's worth knowing all of them before you need one.

The word that matters is compared. Results are compared to documents that say what was expected. If the documents get written after the results are in, nobody is comparing anything. They're describing what happened in a way that lets them do what they'd already decided.

Good criteria have four parts. A measurement, named exactly, with its units and how it's taken. A limit, set from what the thing has to do in service and not from what it did last week. A rule for what each outcome triggers, including the outcome you don't want. And a rule for missing data. The Guide's section on requirements says a requirement, before it's baselined, should be unambiguous, which it defines as measurable and testable. A criterion is a requirement with a deadline on it. Hold it to the same standard.

Where do the limits come from? From the physics, from the hazard, and from the margin you want between them. Not from the data you hope to see. If you set a limit just above last week's worst result, you've written a forecast of a pass and called it a criterion. Look at what failure would mean, work out how much room the system can stand, and pick a limit with margin in it. Then write down the reasoning, so someone can argue with it before the test and not after.
And sign them. The people who'll live with the result should sign the criteria, along with the people who'll decide. A criterion the crew never saw is a criterion the crew didn't agree to.

How the exam asks it. Criteria set after results are seen, or limits chosen to fit the expected result, are distractors. The best answer defines the measurement, the limit and its basis, what each outcome triggers, and how missing data counts, in advance.

The Guide separates two kinds of quality work in section 2.1.6.5. Quality assurance is about using the project's processes well, so that people can trust what comes out. Quality control is about deliverables meeting defined specifications and thresholds. A test is quality control. The criteria, and the discipline of not changing them, are quality assurance. You need both. A perfect test judged by rules invented afterward is worthless, and so is a fine set of rules nobody follows on the day.

When the result comes in, three things are true at once, and people only like to hear one of them. A value inside its limit passes the criterion. A value inside its limit doesn't explain anything. And a value that isn't zero is information. Write all three into the criteria so nobody has to argue about them later. Report every value as measured, beside its limit. Say plainly that passing a criterion makes something eligible for a decision and doesn't make the decision.

That last distinction is the one that saves lives. On a program like this one, a test pass doesn't accept a risk. It tells the people with the authority to accept it that the conditions they set have been met. Then they decide, in writing, and the people exposed to the risk consent, in writing, on the actual data. Consent given before the data isn't consent to the risk. It's consent to a guess about it.

Decide in advance about missing data, too. If a channel drops out, or a reading can't be trusted, the safe rule is that not measured counts as not met. You'll be tempted on the day to say the dropped channel was probably fine. That's the sentence the rule is there to stop.

How the exam asks it. A result inside limits passes the criterion; it doesn't accept the risk or explain the cause. Expect the right answer to report values as measured, apply the preset rule, and leave acceptance with the authority, with consent from those exposed.

In the last month before a launch, a cutover, a go live, or an opening, a project holds readiness reviews, and they go wrong in a predictable way. They turn into presentations. Each lead stands up with slides that say their part is ready, the slides are green, and the open items get read out at the end of the day when everybody wants to go home.

A good readiness review is a comparison, like a gate. Every item has a criterion that says what ready means, the evidence that it's been met, an owner, and a date. Items without evidence are open, whatever anyone's slide says. Closed pending paperwork is open. An item somebody else owns is still on the chart, with the owner's name beside it, because the people reading the chart need to see everything the ship is waiting on, not only the parts that are yours.

The exam outline's R9 asks you to develop the metrics, assess current progress, and help ensure the artifacts are created, reviewed, updated, and kept accessible. The Guide's section on requirements names transition and readiness requirements as their own kind: the training, the procedures, the handovers that have to exist before the work can change hands. A readiness review checks those, too. Ask who'll be running the thing next week and whether they've said, in their own words, that they're ready.

How the exam asks it. In readiness questions, the best answer shows every item against its criterion with evidence, keeps items open until proven closed, and includes items owned by others. Moving an open item off the chart, or reporting it closed pending, is wrong.

Every program gets squeezed at the end. The Guide's section on schedule compression, in section 5, gives you the two tools and their costs. Crashing adds resources to activities on the critical path for the least added cost, and it only works where more people or money actually shorten the activity. Fast tracking runs activities in parallel that would normally run in sequence, and it brings rework and quality risk with it, because the overlap needs more coordination. Neither one changes the scope.

The safe way to compress is to look at what each activity is for. Preparation can often be fast tracked, because doing it early costs only the work if it turns out you didn't need it. Getting ready for a path you may not take is insurance. Testing usually can't be compressed without changing what the test tells you. A cold soak is a condition, not a delay. If you shorten it, you haven't done the test faster. You've done a different test.

The Guide also mentions schedule reserves, and where to put them: where paths come together, so that one late path doesn't push everything after it. A window that runs two weeks past your planned date is a reserve if you declare it as one, and a habit if you don't. Spend it on purpose.

For tracking the squeeze, earned value gives you a schedule variance in money, which is an odd unit for time and goes misleading near the end. Earned schedule, from the practitioner Walt Lipke in 2003, measures it in time. PMI called it an emerging practice in 2005. Earned schedule is the point on the plan where your current earned value was supposed to be reached. SPI(t) is earned schedule divided by actual time. It isn't in the PMBOK Guide, and exam questions rarely use it, but it answers the question everybody's really asking, which is how many days behind are we.

How the exam asks it. When schedule must be recovered near a deadline, fast track preparation and crash where resources truly help. Shortening a test's conditions or cutting verification is the distractor.

The outline's R3 has an enabler most people skip: verify that a measurement system is in place to track benefits. The ship isn't the benefit. The ship is the output. The benefit is what the colony gets from it, measured where the colony is.

The Guide describes the benefits management plan in section 4. It names the target benefits, the timeframe for realizing them, the metrics, the assumptions, the risks, and a benefits owner, the person accountable for monitoring, recording, and reporting the benefits that are actually realized. It also says the plan describes how the value becomes part of ongoing operations. A benefit with no owner after the project closes is a benefit nobody will ever confirm.

Measure the thing itself, not a model of it, once the thing exists. Set the baseline on the day the benefit should start. Pick a timeframe long enough to tell a real gain from a good week. Agree a threshold that triggers action if the measure goes the wrong way. And keep each source of value on its own line. If two things are both making the number go up, and you report them together, you'll credit the wrong one, and in a year somebody will make a decision on that credit.
How the exam asks it. Benefits are measured as outcomes where they occur, against a baseline, by a named owner, over a set timeframe. "Delivered on time" is an output, and so is "installed."

Here's a kind of secret the Code doesn't talk about much. Somebody on your project has been doing something good, quietly, without permission, and now it matters. A spare part nobody registered. A workaround somebody tested on their own time. A storeroom somebody kept stocked because the last storeroom got raided.

Treat it like a risk, because it is one. The Guide calls a risk with a positive effect an opportunity, and in section 5 it gives five ways to respond. Escalate it, if it's outside your scope or authority, to the level whose objectives it affects, and make sure someone there accepts ownership. Exploit it, if you want it to happen for certain. Share it, enhance it, or accept it. Before any of those, though, verify it. An opportunity counted before it's checked is a forecast, and a forecast people lean on is the same danger whether it's good news or bad.

Then there's your own part. If you knew about the secret and didn't say, that's an omission, and the Code's 2.2.5 asks you to report errors and omissions, yours as much as anybody's, to the right authority as soon as you can. The fact that the secret was good doesn't change the duty. The board was making decisions with numbers that left it out. You knew.

Two more lines from the Code are worth having here. The comment on the honesty standards in 5.2 says that when outcomes are positive, we don't take credit for other people's achievements. And 5.2.5 asks us to make an environment where people feel safe to tell the truth. When people hide good things, it's usually because something punished them for trying, and that's a culture to fix, not a person to discipline. If you're the one who made the rule people hid from, say so, in writing, where they can read it.

How the exam asks it. When a hidden asset or opportunity surfaces, verify it before counting it, escalate it to the right owner, disclose any part you played in keeping it quiet, and give the credit to the people who built it.

The days before a big decision are when stakeholders most want to be told something, and when you have least to tell them. The outline's P6 asks you to know what your customers expect and keep their expectations aligned with the outcomes you can actually deliver. Before a test, that means telling them how the result will be judged, what each result would set in motion, and when they'll hear. Then they can watch the result come in without anybody having to interpret it for them.

Resist two temptations. One is the celebration ahead of time, the broadcast with a countdown clock and a big moment built for a pass. The other is silence until it's over. Both leave people to make up their own picture, and the first one makes a bad result worse. Give everyone the same words, at the same time, and keep the people doing the work out of the spectacle.

And look after the team. People under a deadline will work fourteen hour days if you let them, and they'll make the mistakes tired people make. The rehearsal is where you find that out. The Guide calls the review after it a retrospective, and says its outcomes should be actionable, with owners. A rehearsal that finds a problem is a good rehearsal. A retrospective that changes the procedure is a good retrospective. And a team that's allowed to pause on the poll without being thought slow is a team that'll tell you when something's wrong.

How the exam asks it. Before a critical decision, give stakeholders the criteria, what each result means, and when they'll hear, in the same words for everyone. After a rehearsal, run a blameless review and change the process.

The woman with the dog sat with me for most of an hour. I never knew her name. When she got up she said, you looked like somebody who was going to say yes again, and I thought I'd wait till you didn't. Then she walked off down the beach.

That's all nerve is, I've come to think. It's being willing to say no when yes would end the conversation. You can't count on having it on the day. Nobody can. So you write it down beforehand, when it's cheap, and you sign it, and you ask the people who'll fly to sign it too. Then on the day you don't need nerve. You need to read.
How the exam asks it. When in doubt on a gate question: criteria first, data second, decision third, by the people with the authority, in writing.

Wednesday, January 3. 9:00 AM. The board's small room on the fourth floor, not the hearing room. No camera and no gallery, and a whiteboard somebody had cleaned badly, so last month's arrows still showed through like old tire tracks.

Esther Quayle sat at the end of the table with a kitchen timer in front of her. Ruth was two seats down, in the gray cardigan, with the green pen. Lorna Whitcombe had brought her propulsion officer, a young man with a laptop and very straight posture. Garrett and Hana sat for Tallgrass. Sam and Quinn sat for the program. On the screen at the far end, from crew quarters at the Cape, were all four of the crew, and behind Haddad somebody's drawing of a rocket with four stick figures waving from the windows was taped to the wall.

The decision says criteria set with the program, the crew, and flight operations, and published before the test, the chair said. I'd like them published by noon on Friday the twelfth. Nobody in this room knows what MOIV-1 will do on the thirtieth. That's why we're doing this today.

What they did know was on Quinn's first page. Thirty nine completed closes on the ground valve since November. Every third close after a soak had a ripple starting two milliseconds after lift, and the position channels disagreed for a few milliseconds. All of it was inside the ten millisecond ground acceptance limit. Hot fire 2's cycle three at the Cape: seven milliseconds, inside ten. October's forty milliseconds on orbit, on the valve that would fly. Harness revision C against D, unexplained.

Garrett had a proposal on one page, and he presented it well. Use the limits the valve was accepted to. Ten milliseconds, everywhere. If it meets them, the workaround flies. The valve was built to those numbers, and that's the cleanest standard there is. Hana didn't look up from her notes. Ten is a ground acceptance limit for a warm stand. Nobody ever wrote one for a cold valve on orbit. And on orbit it already did forty. Ten fails the valve you're hoping passes.

On the screen Commander Haddad leaned toward the camera. Whatever the numbers are, I'd like to know before we see a trace what each answer does. Inside, then what. Outside, then what. I don't want to be working that out at two in the afternoon on the thirtieth.

Ruth Calder, who'd flown the Petrel and lost it, said one thing, to the table and not to anyone at it. The hardest line to write is the one about what you'll do if you get the answer you don't want. Write that one first. Then she wrote something on her pad and turned it over. Quinn had a draft table from New Year's night in the folder on her knee.
The board needs criteria for the valve test on orbit. What should Sam propose?
A. Back Tallgrass's proposal: the valve's acceptance limits, with a pass meaning the workaround is accepted to fly.
B. Propose that the board set its final limits once the first trace is in, with margin for the unknown.
C. Propose a limit for each measurement and what each outcome triggers, frozen before the trace.
D. Propose a limit for every measurement from the physics and the ground data, and leave near misses for later.

Quinn puts the table on the screen and Sam walks it. Six criteria, each with its measurement, its limit, and a line on where the limit comes from: position disagreement at most fifteen milliseconds, a third of the forty five at which the cutoff sequence calls the valve failed, with the ten millisecond ground limit reported beside it. Pressure confirming the close. MOIV-2 on every cutoff. The procedure as written. The soak, by body temperature. Two blind readers who agree. Then the rules. All met makes the workaround eligible for the board's acceptance, with the crew's consent, and nothing more. Any one missed, or not measured, starts the spacewalk the next morning. Every value gets published as measured. Nothing changes after Friday. Garrett asks where fifteen came from, if not from the ground runs. The chair answers before Sam can. From the cutoff sequence, Mr. Lyle. Forty five milliseconds and a factor of three. It was fifteen before anybody in this room saw a trace, and it would be fifteen whatever the ground runs had shown. She reads the table twice and edits three words. Haddad asks for the eligible line in capitals. Friday the twelfth, then, the chair says, and sets her timer.

That's a go. Write criteria before the data with all four parts: the measurement, the limit and its basis, what each outcome triggers including the one you don't want, and the rule for missing data. Then freeze them. That's how a calm day makes the hard day's decision.
Thursday, January 4. 11:10 AM. The form came from Hale's deputy, with a short note on top and a deadline under it in bold.

ARES RELIEF AUTHORITY CREW RISK CONSENT MOIV-1 (DRAFT FOR SIGNATURE BEFORE CREW LAUNCH). I, THE UNDERSIGNED MEMBER OF THE HALCYON CREW, CONSENT TO FLY MOIV-1 WITH THE CR 62-311 WORKAROUND IF THE INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD ACCEPTS THE RESIDUAL RISK.. SIGNATURE: ________ DATE: ________. RETURN BY 1700 FRIDAY, JANUARY 5.

The note said a consent from orbit would cost a day on January 31, because it needed an uplink, a downlink, and a witness. If the crew signed in quarantine now, the board could accept the risk the afternoon of the test and nobody would lose anything.
Quinn read it over his shoulder. The board's rule says written consent of the crew. It doesn't say when. Hale's office is reading that as anytime.

At 11:40 Haddad called from the Cape. She'd got her copy at the same time he had, and she had the board's draft criteria open beside it, with the word ELIGIBLE in capitals where she'd asked for it. They sent us a form, Sam. Before the data. I'd like to know who's asking us, and what we'd be agreeing to, because I can't tell from this. Behind her, Dr. Rao said something he didn't catch. Haddad turned, and Dr. Rao, the crew's doctor, leaned into the frame. I said four people in quarantine five days before launch aren't the best judges of what they'd sign later. I'm one of them.
Hale's office has sent the crew a consent form. How should Sam handle the consent?
A. Have the crew sign Hale's form in quarantine before launch, as Hale's office asks.
B. Have the crew sign now, on the condition that all six criteria are met on the day.
C. Have Commander Haddad sign the consent for her crew of four, and save the uplinks from orbit.
D. Tell Hale's office consent comes after the test on the real data, and build that step into the plan.

Hale's deputy argues for a day and then stops. Lorna's team builds a ninety minute consent pass into the timeline for the first evening after the board sits: the measured values uplinked by 5 PM on test day, the board's members on the loop, and each crew member asked separately, on a private channel, by the chair, with Dr. Rao asked first about the crew's condition. A no is recorded as a no and nothing else, and the minutes say so in advance. Haddad reads the plan from the Cape. Ask us each. Not me for them.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Consent to a residual risk has to be informed by the actual data, given by each person exposed, with a real choice to refuse. Plan the process in advance so it costs little time on the day; don't move it in front of the data to save that time.
Friday, January 5. 7:30 AM. Flight control at Watkins, the planning room behind Lorna's floor.

Quinn had the on orbit timeline on the wall, from docking on Wednesday, January 10, to the burn on Sunday, February 18. Checkout of the habitat and the Breather module until the 29th. The cold soak from 4 PM on Monday, January 29. The test at 2 PM on the 30th. Then two paths. The workaround, which needed no crew time. The spacewalk, which needed nine days of it: two spacewalks and a retest, January 31 to February 8, if everything for it was ready the morning after the test.

It wasn't ready yet. Getting ready was three and a half days of crew time: suits fit checked, the airlock run through, the replacement valve out of its case and inspected, tools staged, one rehearsal in the trainer. If that waited until after the result, the spacewalk path was thirteen days, not nine.
Hale's office had sent its own idea overnight: cut the soak to eight hours and run the test on Friday the 26th, which would give back four days to whichever path the board chose.

Haddad had sent a request of her own from the Cape, and it was harder to wave off. If the test can run on the 26th, the crew gets three days of rest before burn prep instead of none. We'd like that, if it's safe.

Garrett had his own note, one line. Don't spend 3.5 crew days preparing for a spacewalk we won't need. Lorna Whitcombe, whose team would fly the ship, read it and capped her marker. Whatever we pick goes on my wall by noon, and once it's on my wall it's mine.
The window ran to March 4. The fourteen days after the 18th weren't in anybody's plan as a reserve. They were just where the window ended.
Garrett doesn't want crew days spent on a spacewalk they may not need. What should Sam do with the schedule?
A. Keep the test as written, and fit the spacewalk preparation around it before January 30.
B. Keep the soak and the date, and hold the spacewalk preparation until the result is in.
C. Shorten the cold soak to eight hours and run the test on January 26, four days earlier.
D. Replace the valve by spacewalk now, with the new valve already aboard, and skip the test.

Lorna moves the three and a half days into the checkout weeks, in blocks that don't touch the soak or the test: suits on the 15th, the airlock on the 18th, the valve out of its case on the 22nd, the rehearsal on the 25th. If the test misses, the first spacewalk starts Wednesday morning and the path ends February 8. If it passes, the crew has spent three and a half days on a spacewalk nobody makes. Quinn writes INSURANCE beside the blocks in her own capitals. Garrett reads it and doesn't send another note.

Exactly right. Fast track the preparation, which is cheap to waste, and protect the test, which can't be compressed without changing what it tells you. Keeping both paths ready is what lets the decision be made on the data instead of on the calendar.
Monday, January 8. 9:20 AM. The crew would launch in the morning, and the cards would launch with them.

There were two procedures: the workaround's conditioning cycle and cutoff, revision F, and the January 30 test, which used most of the same steps. They'd be on the crew's tablets and printed on cards in a binder clipped to the bulkhead, because Haddad wanted paper for anything she'd do with her hand on a switch.

At seven Quinn had run the last inspection with flight operations' procedure editor, line by line against the ground runs. She'd found three things. Step 14 commanded MOIV-2 closed before the conditioning cycle finished; on the ground runs it had been after. The crew display labeled MOIV-1's two position channels A and B and didn't say which ran through the revision C harness. And the ripple limit on card 6 still said twelve milliseconds, from a draft in November.
The procedure had been written from Wendell's runs, and some of his notes were still in the margins, in capitals.

Tallgrass's procedures office wanted to fix the three tonight and sign the revision. They're right that it's three lines, Hana said. I'd like to know why we found three today and not in December. Quinn didn't say anything. She'd been asking herself the same thing since seven.
Quinn found three problems in the cards this morning, and the crew launches tomorrow. What should Sam do?
A. Fix the three tonight, have Tallgrass's procedures office sign the revision, and send it up.
B. Fix the three, then walk the whole card with the crew and flight ops before launch.
C. Keep the card as it is through the test to match the ground runs, and fix it after.
D. Send the cards up as they are, and have the crew correct them in pen on orbit.

They do it at eleven that morning, on video with crew quarters at the Cape, every step out loud. At step 22 Brandvold stops them. The callout says MOIV-2 OPEN when the switch it points to reads CLOSE in the cockpit graphic. A fourth. Revision G goes under configuration control at 1:40 PM. On the 17th Lorna's people run it in the ground sim, and on the 18th the crew runs it in the trainer aboard Halcyon, and both runs match the ground valve's sequence step for step. Hana asks the procedures office for a note on why the December review missed three, and gets one.

That's a go. Conduct quality reviews with the people who'll use the deliverable, look for what you haven't found yet as well as fixing what you have, and verify the fix before it's needed. Then ask why the earlier review missed it, which is how quality gets better.

Tuesday, January 9. 4:12 AM in Watkins, 6:12 at the Cape. He watched the crew launch on the big screen in flight control with Lorna's controllers, who didn't clap until the vehicle was in orbit, and then clapped once, together, like a single door closing. Haddad's four kids had been at the viewing site with their father and a sign. The replacement valve rode in its case in the cargo bay. On Wednesday at 7:40 PM the crew docked with Halcyon and opened the hatch, and Haddad's first call down was a pressure reading.
Thursday, January 11. 5:40 AM. The kitchen in Aurora, with the coffee maker going. One way twelve minutes and forty three seconds.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4229. One way, 12 minutes 43 seconds. Margin, 229 days. Hi, Dad. Log fifty nine. Sol 4229. We watched the launch. All of us, in the galley, thirteen minutes behind you. When it cleared the tower Okonkwo cried, which she'll deny, so don't tell her I told you. Yusra's bunk in C ring is made up. Malik put a sign on it that says RESERVED in letters you can read from the hatch. Okay. Here's the log I've been not recording for twenty one months. Bay D is done. I finished it in July, three weeks past your PERT number, which on Mars is early. Racks full, air handler balanced. Mom's peppers are four feet tall in the warm corner, and they're ugly, and they're the best thing up here. It hasn't been in my number for a reason. It runs sealed, on its own handler, because putting a bay on the main loop takes the director's signature, and a bay nobody approved doesn't get one. Sealed, it's starved. Plants need what we breathe out, and the main loop is where all the breathing is. So it's been making a little, and Pilar and I have been putting the little into the two old lander tanks behind it, with a compressor that would give the safety officer a heart attack. The tanks are full. Seventeen days of reserve, by the gauges, which we've read every sol since October. On the main loop it does better. I ran it on the loop six nights in December, on Pilar's shifts, and fit a line. A quarter of a day of air for every day it runs, until the nutrient salts run out, and they run out in ninety six days. That's twenty four. Seventeen and twenty four is forty one. I didn't count it before, because a number they can shut you out of isn't a number, and because six nights is a fit, not a measurement. You taught me that, with the spreadsheets, though you didn't mean to. I'm putting it in now because the ship's coming and the end of the window matters, and because somebody on Earth needs to check my line before anybody leans on it. I told Hollis at seven this morning, in his office, with the gauge log. He didn't say anything for a long time. Then he asked me to show him. The safety officer inspects on Saturday. If it passes, we're on the loop Sunday. Mine's 229 without it. With it, 270. Okonkwo's 236, with it 277. Arrival's day 238. That's plus thirty two. Plus thirty nine. Dad, I've never written plus. Not once since I started counting. And the last day of the window. March fourth, arriving September twentieth. Plus eighteen on mine. Without Bay D it's minus twenty three. That's the one I've been carrying around. Don't count it until somebody checks it. I mean that. Love you. Log fifty nine. Ada out.
He watched it three times. The third time he stopped it on the gauge log in her hands, a spiral notebook with a cover that had been blue once, every page full.

He'd known since April of 2061. She'd told him about the bay in a log, and he'd asked her for three numbers, and she'd given him nine, fourteen, and twenty two months, and he'd written them on a sticky note inside the cabinet door over the coffee maker, where it still was, curling. He'd known in August of that year, when she'd asked him not to hand her over. He'd kept it, because she'd asked him to. He'd never once put it in front of anybody who was making a decision.

For two years he'd been running a ship to rescue her. She'd been building her own way out, a rack at a time, on hours she didn't have, and writing minus nine at the bottom of every log because she wouldn't count what she couldn't prove.
The program's status went to Hale and the board's clerk at noon every Thursday. Its margin line said 236, minus two.
Ada's Bay D could add forty one days to the margin. What should Sam do with that?
A. Wait for Hollis's report and the ARA's check, then count the days, and keep quiet on how long he's known.
B. Add the forty one days to the program's margin in today's status, on Ada's record of being right.
C. Leave Bay D out of the program's reports until after January 30, to protect the valve test.
D. Write Hale and the clerk today that he's known about Bay D from April 2061, and keep the margin as it is.

He writes it at the kitchen table and sends it at 9:12. DISCLOSURE, S. OKAFOR, PROGRAM MANAGER. Five sentences. An unrostered hydroponics bay on Ares Station, built by its own staff, which he's known about since April 2061 from his daughter's personal logs. Its output was never in her stated margin or the program's. He didn't report it. The station's director was told today by the people who built it. He asks the ARA's mission assurance office to check the bay's data before the program counts a day of it. Hale calls at 9:30 and is angry for four minutes, then asks how sure anybody is. He says that's not his to be sure of. At the program room Quinn reads the memo, says nothing, and draws a second line on the margin chart in pencil, dotted, and writes UNVERIFIED beside it. That night he records a log at the kitchen table and doesn't play it back first. I told Hale this morning that I've known about Bay D since April of '61. I'm telling you the same day. You wrote plus. I've watched it four times now. I've been building a ship to come get you, and you've been building the door.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Escalate an opportunity to the owners whose objectives it affects, and verify it before anyone counts it. Disclose your own omission plainly (Code 2.2.5, 5.3.1), and leave the credit with the people who built it.
Monday, January 15. 6:30 AM. Hollis Bayne's Monday report posted to the ARA's site, the way it had every Monday for three years. It was longer than usual.

ARES STATION DIRECTOR'S WEEKLY REPORT TO THE ARA MONDAY, JANUARY 15, 2063 (EXTRACT). OXYGEN PLANT OPERATING WITHIN PROJECTED DEGRADATION.. MARGIN: 232 DAYS (ARA MODEL).. BAY D (HYDROPONICS, C RING): AN UNAUTHORIZED MODIFICATION, BUILT BY A. OKAFOR AND HER TEAM. REPORTED TO THIS OFFICE BY ITS BUILDER, SOL 4229. INSPECTED BY STATION SAFETY, SOL 4231. ACCEPTED WITH THREE CORRECTIONS: COMPRESSOR RELOCATED, TANK RELIEF VALVES REPLACED, FIRE DETECTION ADDED. TIED INTO THE MAIN AIR LOOP, SOL 4232.. CREDIT: 41 DAYS (17 STORED, BY GAUGE; 24 PROJECTED). NOT INCLUDED IN THE MARGIN ABOVE. PENDING ARA MISSION ASSURANCE REVIEW.. A. OKAFOR IS NAMED BAY D LEAD. A NOTE OF THE UNAUTHORIZED WORK IS IN HER FILE. A NOTE IS IN MINE.. SHE HID IT BECAUSE I WOULD HAVE SHUT IT. THE RULE THAT MADE THAT TRUE WAS MINE, AND IT IS WITHDRAWN. ANY RESIDENT MAY NOW PROPOSE A MODIFICATION TO THIS OFFICE AND WILL HAVE AN ANSWER IN SEVEN SOLS.. MORALE: I HAVE WRITTEN STRONG IN THIS LINE FOR THREE YEARS. THIS WEEK IT IS BETTER THAN THAT.

Sam read it twice at the counter. Beside it was page fourteen, which had come on Saturday in a long white envelope with a Golden postmark, posted the afternoon the board's criteria went up on Friday and not an hour before. He'd read the 1001 line standing exactly where he was standing now.

Ruth had called on Sunday night, which she'd never done about the board's business. She kept it to the criteria. I voted for them. I've read them four times since, and I'm going to stop. Read them once more before the thirtieth, Sam, and then don't read them again until the numbers are in. Don't let anybody read them to you on the day. He said he wouldn't. That's all. Good night. She hung up before he could ask her anything, and he hadn't been going to.

At the program room Quinn had the station's engineering packet up. Okonkwo's team had sent it on January 8, before the crew left Earth, and item two named the station's benefits owner: Chiamaka Okonkwo, Breather operations, reporting through the director's packet. Item three was a question. Bay D changes the arithmetic. If its air is counted in the Breather's number, Earth will think the plant is better than it is. If the plant's air is counted in Bay D's, Ada gets a statue. Which line is which?
Whatever had been said in December about what success was, nobody had written down how to count air from two places.

There were other ideas. Hale's program office wanted the benefit reported as Halcyon delivered and the Breather installed by September 6, with a box to tick. Hollis's office had sent a single figure: station margin above 180 days on the ninetieth sol after arrival. The ARA's model, rebuilt in July, could compute a benefit from Earth without anybody on the station lifting a pen. Halcyon's cargo module carried seed stock and nutrient salts, so Bay D would start again when the ship arrived, and its air would go into the same tanks as the Breather's.
Under the packet, Quinn had pinned his disclosure memo from Thursday. Somebody at the ARA had written VERIFYING in the margin.
Hale's office, Hollis and the ARA each want a different benefit measure. How should Sam track it?
A. Measure the benefit as the ship arriving on September 6, with the Breather installed and running.
B. Report the benefit after arrival from the board's checked model, to spare the station the work.
C. Count Bay D's days inside the Breather's benefit, read each sol as one figure for air at Ares Station.
D. Have Okonkwo own a reading of the reserve from the plant log each sol, with Bay D on its own line.

It takes two packets, because the station answers a day later. What comes back is a half page and a table. The baseline is the reserve on the day the Breather starts. The measure is the reserve itself, read from the station's plant log every sol, not the model. Bay D gets its own line, and so does the Breather, so that neither borrows the other's air. The target is the reserve rising instead of falling for ninety sols. Two sols of falling reserve in a row triggers a review with Lorna's team. Okonkwo owns it and reports every week through the director's packet to the board; assumptions and risks are listed underneath, salts and spares and gauge drift among them. Hollis signs the packet. Okonkwo's reply has a line at the bottom. Understood as: we measure air, not ships.

Exactly right. Verify that a measurement system is in place to track the benefit: the outcome measured where it happens, against a baseline, by a named owner, over a set timeframe, with each source of value kept separate so credit and decisions land in the right place.

Wednesday, January 17. 8:00 AM. Flight control. The crew had been aboard Halcyon for a week, and Lorna had a number on her whiteboard in red: 84. Crew hours left before the soak, outside the checkout and the spacewalk preparation.
Under it, Quinn had stuck up nine cards, one for each request that had come in since launch. Each said who wanted it and how many crew hours it took.

CREW TIME REQUESTS JAN 17 TO JAN 29 84 HOURS AVAILABLE. 1. FULL REGRESSION, FLIGHT LOAD 11.6, ON THE FLIGHT COMPUTERS (RAFA, THANDI): 6. 2. BREATHER MODULE THERMAL CHECKOUT (PALOMA'S TEAM): 12. 3. LANDER HEALTH CHECK (LANDER TEAM): 8. 4. CABIN CAMERA INSTALL FOR THE BURN BROADCAST (ARA PUBLIC AFFAIRS): 10. 5. SECOND SPACEWALK REHEARSAL (EVA TEAM): 16. 6. MEDICAL BASELINES (DR. RAO): 6. 7. BACKUP COMMUNICATIONS PATH TEST (FLIGHT OPS): 8. 8. HABITAT STOWAGE AUDIT (CARGO TEAM): 20. 9. CARGO PHOTO SURVEY FOR THE FAMILIES' NEWSLETTER (FAMILIES OF ARES): 5. TOTAL: 91 HOURS. OVER BY 7. PLUS 40 FOR ITEMS 2 AND 8 IF THEY'RE DONE THE WAY THEIR TEAMS WANT.
Really it was a hundred and thirty one, because the Breather team and the cargo team had each sent a short version and a long one.
Item one had been on every list since the workaround was approved. Thandi wanted all six hours, on the flight computers, not the bench.

On the screen from orbit, Haddad had her sleeves pushed up and a pen clipped to her collar. We'll do whatever's on the list. I'd like the list to be the right list. Beside her, Mateo Echeverría, the flight engineer, held up a hand with a bandage on one thumb, from a stowage latch. And not fourteen hour days. We tried one Tuesday. By the end of it I'd stowed a wrench in the trash bag.
There are eighty four crew hours left and nine requests for them. How should Sam decide what fits?
A. Let Tallgrass's engineers choose which items go, as the people who know the ship's systems best.
B. Rank the nine with the crew and flight ops by what each would change before the burn.
C. Ask every requesting team to cut its own request by a third, and fit the total that way.
D. Fit all nine by moving the crew to fourteen hour days through the twenty ninth.

They go card by card, with Haddad on the screen and Lorna at the board, and ask one question of each: if this found a problem, would anybody decide anything differently before the burn? Regression: yes, it's the burn's software, all six hours on the flight computers. The second spacewalk rehearsal: yes. The Breather's thermal checkout, short version: yes. Backup communications: yes. Medical baselines: yes, Dr. Rao says, flatly. The lander check moves to cruise week two. Half the stowage audit and the photo survey go to cruise too. The cabin camera comes out, and Sam calls Hale's office himself before lunch to say why. Fifty eight hours of eighty four. Haddad initials the board from orbit, which is to say she holds up her initials on a card and Quinn copies them.

That's a go. Prioritize work by value with the key stakeholders. On a deadline, value means what an item would change in the decisions ahead, so keep what informs the go/no-go and defer what doesn't, openly.

Friday, January 19. 9:00 AM. The ARA's integrated readiness review, the last one before the poll, in the big room at flight control. Hale in the chair for the agency. Lorna, Garrett, Hana, Corinne, Rafa, the crew on the loop, two of the partners' liaisons, and an observer from the board's staff at the back with a notebook.

The first item wasn't on the agenda. The ARA's mission assurance office had checked Bay D's gauge log and the six night runs, and it adopted the forty one days at 9:05, with a footnote: seventeen days verified by gauge, twenty four projected and to be remeasured every week. The agency's figure went from 228 to 269. Arrival was day 230. Plus thirty nine, the first plus on the ARA's line since July. Hale read the footnote out loud and then the name in it, and didn't look at Sam.

Then Quinn's tracker, twenty three open items. Most were small. One belonged to the ARA's sustainability office. After the burn, the spent departure stage had to be pushed onto a heliocentric disposal path, with propellant set aside for it. The plan for that was written and costed, and not yet signed. Four said CLOSED PENDING PAPERWORK. One was I-62-117, MOIV-1, with the test date beside it.
Hana's slide on it said what it had said since November. The lot valve's runs had ruled out two more causes and found none.

Garrett had a proposal for the chart, and he put it kindly. The program's ready. The valve is the board's call, not ours. Put I-62-117 on the board's list where it belongs, close the four that are only waiting on signatures, and let the partners see what we've actually built. One green box, Sam. They've earned one. One of the liaisons nodded.
Garrett wants one green box for the partners. How should Sam run the readiness review?
A. Show the program as ready, move I-62-117 to the board's list, and close the four awaiting signatures.
B. Postpone the review until after the thirtieth, and hold one review then for the whole ship.
C. Show all twenty three items against their criteria and evidence, the valve included.
D. Run the review as a briefing from each team lead in turn, and collect the open items at the end.

Quinn puts all twenty three on one screen, each with its criterion, its evidence, its owner, and its date. The four closed pending paperwork go back to open, and three of them close by Tuesday with the paperwork in hand. I-62-117 sits in the middle, open, with the test on the 30th, Rule A and Rule B beside it, and each path's dates. Lorna says two of her own conditions are still open and reads them out. Hale reads the screen top to bottom, the way she'd count a roll call, and asks the liaisons to take a picture of this one. Garrett gets no green box. At the break he tells Corinne it's a better chart than the one he wanted, which Corinne writes on her legal pad.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. A readiness review compares each item to its criterion, with evidence, owner, and date. Open means open until proven closed, and items owned by others stay visible. That's what makes status something people can act on.

Tuesday, January 23. 1:00 PM. The full countdown rehearsal for the burn, in flight control, with Lorna's twelve controllers, the program's consoles, and the crew on the loop from orbit. Quinn ran it from the countdown lead's desk with the procedure open in front of her and a cup of tea she forgot about at 1:05. Brandvold flew the simulated burn.

At T minus twenty minutes Quinn called the poll. Each station answered in turn. When she got to propulsion, Arlo, at Wendell's old console, said, Prop is and stopped, and then said, go, and Quinn moved on to guidance, because the next name on her sheet was guidance.

At simulated cutoff, MOIV-2 closed on command. Lorna had put in a failure nobody knew about: channel B on MOIV-1 dropped out at cutoff. Two consoles missed it for forty seconds, because three people were talking on the loop at once. It turned out Quinn's poll sheet listed the stations in a different order from the procedure, which nobody had noticed in four practice runs.

Afterward, in the hall by the vending machine, Arlo found Sam. I had a question about MOIV-2's data rate. That was the pause. I didn't want to hold up the poll. It was a sim. He tucked his hands into his jacket. I'd have asked it on the real one. Probably.
Sam stood there with a bag of pretzels he didn't want and thought about page ten, and the second somebody had heard in 2035 and never asked about.

The rehearsal's list had fourteen items on it by four o'clock. Friday's second rehearsal was on the timeline, and Hale's office had asked by email whether it could go, since it took three hours of the crew's attention four days before the test.
The rehearsal turned up fourteen items, and Hale's office wants to cancel Friday's second rehearsal. What's Sam's best move?
A. Cancel Friday's second rehearsal, as Hale's office asked, and give the crew those hours back.
B. Fix the fourteen items, brief every console by email, and run Friday's rehearsal as planned.
C. Hold a blameless review with every console tonight, and write what it finds into the procedure.
D. Talk to Arlo privately about the pause, and have Hana sit propulsion for Friday and the real poll.

They do it at seven in the controllers' break room, with pizza, and Lorna says the ground rule before anyone sits down: nobody here is in trouble. What did you see, and what did you need? Arlo tells the room about the pause himself. Lorna says she's done the same thing twice, on lander polls, and never told anybody. Three changes come out of it. Any console may answer hold, question, and it doesn't count against the go/no-go. The countdown lead asks any pause to say again its status. One voice on the loop during the poll; side questions go to a second loop. Quinn writes them into the countdown procedure that night and sends them to the ARA's procedures office as a change to its standard countdown, for every ship after this one. On Friday two consoles pause, and Quinn asks each of them to say again. Both times it's nothing. Ilse Brandvold, the pilot, says on the loop, Flight, crew. Same rule up here. If one of us pauses, ask.

Exactly right. Use what the rehearsal taught: a blameless review with the people involved, specific changes with owners, the procedure updated so the next team inherits the fix, and a second rehearsal to prove it works. That's continuous improvement and an OPA update together.
Decision ten. Two and a half days.
Thursday, January 25. 6:00 AM. Quinn had been in since five, and the chart on her screen had two lines on it that had come apart.

The crew's checkout plan was four hundred task points from January 10 to January 29, twenty days. At the end of Wednesday, day fifteen, they'd earned 236. The plan said 284. On the plan, 236 had been due halfway through day thirteen.

Crew checkout: planned points by end of day, and earned at day 15. Plan: 400 points from Wed Jan 10 (day 1) to Mon Jan 29 (day 20). Earned at the end of day 15, Wed Jan 24: 236. Of the 164 points left, 41 must be done before the soak starts at 4 PM on the 29th; they're on plan.

It had started on Saturday with a coolant pump on the habitat's loop B, which had begun to make a noise like gravel in a coffee can. Echeverría had spent nineteen hours on it over three days and fixed it, and two of his fingers were still taped. The medical baselines had taken twice as long as planned, because Dr. Rao didn't skip things.
The work that had to be done before the soak was on plan; Quinn had kept it that way on purpose. The rest of the checkout wasn't.

Garrett's note proposed fourteen hour days through Monday. Hale's office asked whether the test could move to Saturday, February 3. Corinne had sent a text at 5:52. My second shift can take every bit of telemetry reduction and procedure prep the crew's doing by hand. Twenty two points. Say the word. Lorna had a list of her own on the whiteboard, headed NOT NEEDED BEFORE THE BURN. Some of it had been on the list since the day they sorted the eighty four hours.
The crew's checkout is running two and a half days behind plan. How should Sam respond?
A. Move what the burn doesn't need into cruise with flight ops, and give ground work to Corinne's shift.
B. Skip the habitat checkout tasks that already passed in ground acceptance before launch.
C. Ask the board to move the test to Saturday, February 3, and finish the checkout first.
D. Put the crew on fourteen hour days through the twenty ninth to finish the checkout before the soak.

Lorna and Haddad go through the 123 points that aren't test critical, line by line, on the loop. Fifty eight aren't needed before the burn, and they move to cruise weeks one to three, owned by flight ops in writing. Corinne's second shift at Watkins takes twenty two more off the crew: telemetry reduction and the procedure prep they'd been doing by hand. The crew stays on ten hour days, and Dr. Rao's rest rule holds. Quinn redraws the chart with two plans on it, one for before the burn and one for cruise, and the line for before the burn meets its plan on February 1. The forty one test critical points finish Sunday, a day early.

That's a go. Analyze the variance, then compress what's safe: protect the critical path to the test, re-sequence work the deadline doesn't need, and add resources where they actually shorten the work. Keep the people doing it rested.
Friday, January 26. 10:00 AM. Hale's office had a plan for Monday night, and it came with a run of show.

A press event in Denver at seven, with families in the front rows. The first item: ARA SUPPORTED STATION INITIATIVE EXTENDS COLONY MARGIN BY 41 DAYS. The second: a live broadcast of Tuesday's test from Halcyon's cabin, with a countdown graphic and Commander Haddad narrating each close. The cabin camera was already out of the crew's timeline, so the plan said the camera would go back in.
Simon Greaves had sent one line at 9:15. What happens Tuesday if it's fourteen milliseconds?

Frances Odum called at 9:40. The families in her group had two hundred questions, she said, and most of them were one question: what does Tuesday mean? And there was a second thing. The station families have been sending messages home all week about a bay full of peppers. They call it Ada's bay. Is it real, and why isn't her name on anything the agency's put out?
It was in Hollis's report. It wasn't in Hale's run of show.
Frances asks what Tuesday means, and why Ada's name isn't on anything the agency's put out. How should Sam answer?
A. Send the families and the press one page on how Tuesday will be judged, at the same hour.
B. Tell the families that with forty one more days of margin, Tuesday's test matters less now.
C. Say nothing more to the families or the press until the board rules on the result.
D. Run Monday's event as Hale's office planned it, with the live broadcast and the margin news first.

It takes two calls with Hale and one with Lorna. What goes out is one page, at the same hour, to the families' list and the press: the six criteria, the four rules, both paths and their dates, and when people will hear. Measured values by 6 PM Tuesday, the board's ruling when it sits, and Sam on the families' line the same day it posts. The forty one days are credited to Ada Okafor and the Bay D team on Ares Station, with the station director's safety staff, measured there and checked by the ARA's mission assurance office. There's no cabin camera. The crew works, and the public feed carries flight control's own loop. Greaves runs the page in full on Countdown to Ares and answers his own question on air. Fourteen would pass C1, and it wouldn't explain the valve, and they told us so first. Frances texts at 8:40 PM. They're calling it Ada's bay. I told them that's what it's called.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Before a critical decision, manage expectations with the truth: how the result will be judged, what each outcome triggers, and when they'll hear, in the same words for everyone at once. Credit good news to the people who earned it (Code 5.2, comment).
Monday, January 29. 4:00 PM. On orbit, MOIV-1's heaters went off, and the cold soak began. Twenty two hours. Over the high bay doors the clock said 20.

In flight control the room had split without anybody deciding it would. Rafa's team had a sprint goal on their whiteboard in green marker: SPRINT GOAL: TEST PASSES 1/30. Somebody in Tallgrass's propulsion group had ordered T shirts that said PASS IT, and a box of them was open on a chair. Garrett hadn't ordered them, and had said so, and was wearing one.

At the far end of the room the spacewalk support team sat together with their checklists and didn't wear the shirts. One of them had been called the plan B people in a meeting, and it had stuck. They'd spent three and a half crew days getting ready for a morning that might not come.
On the loop from orbit, Brandvold asked it plainly. Flight, crew. Question for the program. Are we hoping tomorrow, or testing?
Hana was at her desk with the lot data and her coat on, not leaving.
Brandvold asks the program a plain question: are we hoping tomorrow, or testing? What should Sam do tonight?
A. Tell the team tonight that the ground runs point to a pass, and let them go home on that.
B. Get everyone into the room tonight, with the crew on the loop, to say what the test is for.
C. Send every team a short note tonight restating the vision and the published criteria.
D. Let each team keep its own goal for tomorrow, as each has a different job on the test.

At seven he gets everyone who'll fit into the room, with the crew on the loop, and takes five minutes. The test is to find out what the valve does. A pass makes the workaround eligible and the board decides. A miss starts the spacewalk at six on Wednesday, and the ship still leaves inside the window. Nobody in this room is on the losing side of tomorrow, and the spacewalk team are the reason a miss isn't a disaster. The goal hasn't changed since January of 2061. It's air at Ares Station. Rafa wipes his whiteboard with his sleeve and writes, SPRINT GOAL: CLEAN DATA 1/30. The T shirts go back in their box, and somebody tapes the box shut. Haddad comes on the loop. Copy. We're testing. Brandvold says, Then I'll read the card twice and go to sleep.

Exactly right. When the root cause of a misunderstanding is that each group pictures success as its own result, restate the shared vision with everyone at once: what the work is for, why every path serves it, and what success really is.

Tuesday, January 30. 12:40 PM. Flight control at Watkins, with the wind sock straight out toward Kansas and every chair in the room taken. On the big screen, beside the countdown clock at 19, the criteria that had posted on the twelfth, with the signatures under them. E. QUAYLE FOR THE BOARD S. OKAFOR FOR THE PROGRAM Y. HADDAD FOR THE CREW L. WHITCOMBE FOR FLIGHT OPERATIONS Quinn had drafted the table on New Year's night. The three words the chair had edited were still in the chair's handwriting.

The soak was twenty hours and forty minutes old. MOIV-1's body temperature read where Hana had said it would, and she'd stopped looking at it every thirty seconds and started looking at it every minute.
Rafa's whiteboard said CLEAN DATA 1/30. The box of shirts was under a desk with tape on it.

At 1:30 Wendell came in. Nobody had asked him. He had his canvas jacket on and page twelve in his shirt pocket, behind the doctor's note, and he sat in the back row by the coffee and said to the controller next to him that he'd come to hear it. Arlo saw him from the propulsion console and touched the headset at his ear, and Wendell lifted two fingers off his knee. Nobody asked him anything, and he didn't offer.
Downtown, the board watched from the fourth floor, on the same feed.

At 1:50 Quinn polled the room for the start of the test. At propulsion Arlo said, Prop is go, without a pause. At guidance there was one, a short one, and Quinn said, Guidance, say again your status. It was a headset cable. Everyone in the room heard her ask.
At 1:58 the conditioning cycle ran, exactly as the card said. At 2:00 Haddad's voice came down from orbit, flat and clear. Flight, Halcyon. Close one, on my mark. Mark.

Close one, clean. Close two, clean. The two blind readers at flight operations' propulsion desk sat with their backs to the big screen and their own traces in front of them and wrote on their pads, each turned so the other couldn't see.

Close three. The pressure trace rippled, two milliseconds after lift, the way it had on the ground, the way everybody in the room could have drawn it from memory. The two position channels disagreed for a little while and then agreed again. Downstream pressure said closed at thirty four milliseconds. On orbit MOIV-2 closed on command. Nobody in the room said anything at all.
Close four, clean. Close five, clean. At 2:31 the readers turned their pads over, and they'd both written the same thing beside close three.

INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD ITEM 1 FINAL INTEGRATED TEST OF MOIV-1 RESULTS AS MEASURED TUESDAY, JANUARY 30, 2063, 1431. SOAK: 22 HOURS 0 MINUTES BY BODY TEMPERATURE. CLOSES: 5 COMMANDED, 5 COMPLETED.. C1 POSITION DISAGREEMENT, LIMIT 15 MS: CLOSES 1, 2, 4, 5 UNDER 1 MS. CLOSE 3: 12 MS. MET. GROUND ACCEPTANCE LIMIT 10 MS: CLOSE 3 ABOVE IT, REPORTED.. C2 PRESSURE CONFIRMS CLOSED, LIMIT 50 MS: WORST 34 MS, CLOSE 3. MET.. C3 MOIV-2 ON COMMAND AT EVERY CUTOFF: 5 OF 5. MET.. C4 PROCEDURE AS WRITTEN: MET.. C5 SOAK AT LEAST 20 HOURS: MET.. C6 ALL CHANNELS RECORDED, TWO BLIND READERS AGREE: MET. BOTH READERS CALL CLOSE 3.. RIPPLE FROM 2 MS AFTER LIFT, CLOSE 3 ONLY.. RULE A APPLIES. THE WORKAROUND IS ELIGIBLE FOR THE BOARD'S WRITTEN RISK ACCEPTANCE, WITH THE CREW'S WRITTEN CONSENT. ELIGIBLE ISN'T ACCEPTED.. RULE C. CLOSE 3 IS PUBLISHED AS MEASURED. IT PASSES C1. IT DOESN'T EXPLAIN THE VALVE.. THE BOARD WILL SIT ON THE RESULT.
Lorna told the spacewalk team to keep the suits charged and the valve out of its case until the board said otherwise. They'd done the preparation for a morning that hadn't come yet, and might still.
The consent pass was on the timeline, ninety minutes long, unopened, waiting for whenever the board sat: each of the four, separately, on a private channel, with the data in front of them.

At 5:50 the results page went to the families' list and the press in the same minute, the way he'd said it would. He called Frances at six. She'd already read it twice. Twelve, and the limit's fifteen, and it doesn't explain anything. I can say that. That's what you told us it would look like.
Eleven minutes after the readers turned their pads over, it was on every screen in the galley on Ares Station.
He'd spent the month writing things down before he knew how they'd come out. It hadn't felt brave. It had felt like paperwork, which Ruth would have said was the point.
That evening Quinn walked back across the road to the program room, to the whiteboard where the box said TEST TUE JAN 30, and under it, in her small capitals, she wrote one number.
Twelve milliseconds on the third close. Inside the limit the board wrote. Above the one the valve was accepted to on the ground. And not zero.
